summary: A web platform built with micro-services architecture, dedicated to the study of flames in microgravity conditions, designed for students, academics, or simply curious individuals. It features an interactive dashboard with an integrated AI virtual assistant powered by RAG, providing context in the study area. The platform also includes a ranking of NASA publications and research, sortable by study environment, among other variables of interest to facilitate the discovery of research papers. Finally, the application offers a prediction tool trained on FLEX data to determine whether a flame will extinguish, and this dataset is available for free download.
details:
Our project is a web platform that turns NASA's microgravity combustion research into answers that engineers, mission planners and the public can use. It draws on the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive.

The home screen is the night sky over Chile's Elqui Valley. Each star of the Southern Cross opens one part of the app:

  • Mission: why fire behaves differently when nothing falls. In free fall a candle flame becomes a faint blue sphere instead of a teardrop.
  • Investigation: what NASA has learned about preventing, detecting and suppressing fires in spacecraft.
  • Library: NASA combustion investigations, organized by fire-safety pillar and by relevance to each habitat (spacecraft, station, Moon base, pressurized rover).
  • Flame Lab: a simulator where you set the fuel, cabin pressure, oxygen level, suppressant gas and droplet size and a machine-learning models trained on 274 real droplet-combustion tests from the ISS (FLEX, PSI-69) redict two things: whether the flame will go out on its own, and how early.

An AI assistant answers questions in plain language. It searches a corpus of 305 NASA documents from 24 investigations and cites its sources.

How it works

  • Models. A classifier predicts extinction, a gradient-boosting regressor predicts the droplet diameter when the flame goes out. Both were validated with grouped cross-validation (5 folds × 10 repeats), grouped by atmosphere, so tests from the same chamber fill never appear on both sides of a split. The classifier reaches a macro-F1 of 0.79 and a ROC-AUC of 0.89. A model only ships if it beats a simpler baseline.
  • Honesty layer. A nearest-neighbor index tells the user whether the chosen combination was ever tested, how many real tests sit close to it, which five are closest, and how much to trust the answer (high, medium or low).
  • Assistant. It combines keyword search with semantic search (bge-small embeddings) and answers through a language model. Numbers always come from the models and the data, never from the language model.

What the data revealed

  • The ghost flame. In 53 of 60 heptane tests where the visible flame went out, investigators recorded "cool flames". In test FLEX-035, the visible flame lasted 9 seconds, yet the droplet kept burning invisibly for 27 more seconds and consumed 62 % of its fuel.
  • Moon-base air. In air like the one planned for lunar habitats (about 0.7 atm and at least 30 % oxygen), none of the 17 FLEX flames went out on their own.
  • A gap. No FLEX test used a suppressant gas above 25 % oxygen. Putting out a fire in lunar-habitat air has not been tested in this dataset.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Speed. Decades of experiments, spread across thousands of files written for specialists, become answers in seconds, with every answer traceable to a NASA source.
  • Safer habitat design. It shows what the evidence says about fire in the atmospheres planned for the Artemis era, and where that evidence ends.
  • Pointing to the next experiment. By mapping what has never been tested, it shows which experiment is still missing.
  • Replicable. The same recipe (scientific archive → cited answers → honest models → map of gaps) applies to Mars missions and to oxygen-rich closed spaces on Earth, such as submarines and hyperbaric chambers.

Tools and technologies

Area

Tools

Frontend

React 19, TypeScript, Vite+, TanStack Router and Query, Motion

API gateway

NestJS (TypeScript)

Assistant service

Node.js, TypeScript, Model Context Protocol, SQLite with FTS5 and sqlite-vec, any OpenAI-compatible language model (Ollama for local runs)

ML service

Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy, sentence-transformers

Training and corpus pipelines

Python, pytest, PyMuPDF, YAML configs, versioned artifacts with data hashes

Deployment

Docker Compose

Data

NASA PSI: the FLEX experimental table, test sheets and real camera frames, plus documents from BASS, BASS-II, Saffire, SAME, FLEX-2, ACME and other investigations

What makes it creative

  • Navigation by the Southern Cross, seen from the Elqui Valley, one of the darkest skies on Earth and home to world-class observatories. It reflects where our team comes from.
  • A visual language for gravity. Blue always means microgravity and amber means gravity, across the whole app.
  • Honesty as a feature. Most AI tools answer confidently even without data. Ours shows how much real evidence backs each prediction and says plainly when a combination was never tested. Our motto: "We know where our knowledge ends."
  • Real NASA imagery. We show the actual ISS camera frames, including the "ghost flame", not illustrations.

Factors we considered

  • Scarce data. We did not use synthetic data or augmentation. We report how much evidence supports each prediction instead.
  • The gravity gap. PSI has no partial-gravity combustion data, so predictions are labeled "microgravity only" and Moon or Mars gravity is never presented as measured.
  • Honest validation. Grouped splits keep accuracy from looking better than it is.
  • No invented numbers. The language model explains; the models and the data supply the numbers.
  • Target atmospheres. ISS (21 % O₂ at 14.7 psi), Moon base and rovers (at least 30 % O₂ at no more than 10.2 psi) and spacesuits (100 % O₂ at 4.3 psi).
  • Audience and access. The app has to make sense to non-specialists, cite every source, and work with reduced motion and keyboard-only navigation.
